title: "Litigation Often Takes a Toll on a Party's Mental Health on Both Sides of the 'v'"
content:
From Doe v. Simons, decided July 29 by Judge Nicholas Ranjan (W.D. Pa.):

Plaintiff John Doe has moved to proceed under a pseudonym. Doe advances three main bases for anonymity: his mental illness; that requiring him to litigate under his own name would deter him, and similarly situated individuals, from pursuing litigation; and that his HIPAA-protected medical records would become public….

Doe has not shown that he faces a reasonable fear of severe harm. Doe's case appears to be a straightforward employment-discrimination case. And where plaintiffs allege a fear of severe harm (namely heightened mental illness symptoms and stigma) in ordinary employment-discrimination cases, like this case, courts have denied motions to proceed under a pseudonym. See Doe v. Coll. of New Jersey (3d Cir. 2021) (affirming district court's denial of plaintiff's motion to proceed pseudonymously where the district court … "observed that, with regard to a need for anonymity, [plaintiff's] case was not meaningfully different from other employment disputes"). This Court has seen many cases like this one, and recognizes that litigation often takes a toll on a party's mental health on both sides of the "v."

But the mental-health effects of litigation are, in a sense, the cost of doing business. Doe has not shown the Court that the mental-health effects of this particular lawsuit are so exceptional compared to other similar cases where plaintiffs have proceeded under their legal names. See Kimberly Davis v. Surefire Hospitality Group (W.D. Pa. 2026) ("[T]he distress [here] is more properly characterized as embarrassment or discomfort, which the Third Circuit has found to be insufficient to meet the standard. Without particularized allegations, Plaintiff's request reflects a personal preference, rather than a reasonable fear or severe harm.")….

[O]ne of [Doe's] main concerns is that his sensitive, HIPAA-protected medical information will be publicly disclosed. But the Court has already granted several of Doe's motions to file documents under seal. And many similarly situated individuals have filed lawsuits within this district. The Court stresses one of the most important [factors related to pseudonymity litigation]—that there is a universal public interest in the identities of litigants—and notes that this factor significantly outweighs Doe's alleged fear of severe harm….

title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges and admits shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO
content:
News

Mandatory Credit: Photo by SARAH YENESEL/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock (16049970a) New York, New York, USA, 08 December 2025.

Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges and admits shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO

Luigi Mangione on Friday has pleaded guilty to the two remaining charges against him in the death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in December 2024. The charges of interstate stalking resulting in death and stalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death, filed in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, both have a maximum penalty of life in prison without parole.

“I shot Mr. Thompson and he died. I knew what I was doing was illegal,” Mangione told the court during his allocution. He also said that he had never been treated or hospitalized for any mental illness or addiction, and that his mind was clear during the hearing.

Mangione does not have a plea deal with the federal government. Instead, he will face sentencing on December 18. Federal prosecutor Jamie McDonald said that the government would seek life imprisonment.

On January 30, Judge Margaret Garnett threw out two of the four charges against Mangione, including “murder through use of a firearm during and in relation to the stalking crimes charged…” A conviction on this charge would have made Mangione eligible for the death penalty.

Mangione still faces state charges in the case, scheduled for September 8. Mangione’s defense lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, filed a motion to dismiss the state’s second-degree murder and firearms charges, arguing a violation of due process and double jeopardy.

New York’s double jeopardy (when previous prosecution bars subsequent prosecution) statute is broader than the protection offered by the US Constitution. However, it includes nine narrow exceptions. Friedman Agnifilo’s motion argues that none of the exceptions apply, but she preemptively challenged CPL § 40.20(2)(b), “Each of the offenses as defined contains an element which is not an element of the other, and the statutory provisions defining such offenses are designed to prevent very different kinds of harm…” and 40.20(2)(f), “One of the offenses consists of a violation of a…provision of another jurisdiction, which offense has been prosecuted…and …been terminated by a court order…founded upon insufficiency of evidence to establish some element of such offense which is not an element of the other offense.”

In court for his guilty plea, Mangione for the first time described how he learned where UnitedHealthcare would hold its annual investor convergence in December 2024. He also learned who would attend. Mangione said that he printed a gun with a 3-D printer and affixed it with a silencer (suppressor). Defense attorney Friedman Agnifilo said that Mangione took full responsibility for Thompson’s death.

title: After many hours with Star Wars: Zero Company, I know it'll be brilliant for one very simple reason: XCOM is brilliant too
author: Chris Tapsell
content:
"Honestly, you couldn't believe that this hadn't been done before."

There's a funny thing with video game genres in particular: a lot of them are based on just closely tracing the lines of preexisting games, only with a few small mechanical tweaks and a different-enough setting over the top. And few genres are quite as obvious in that regard as the XCOM-alike: a turn-based tactics game based on managing a small squad of permanently-killable allies through a series of close-quarters, grid-based combat encounters, before ducking out to do a bit of RPG-lite housework in some kind of base or mothership metagame. This is Star Wars: Zero Company, a game where you do all of that, but it's Star Wars. And obviously it's completely brilliant.

I say obviously because this is the magic with this sort of thing: XCOM is completely brilliant, the modern Firaxis iterations in particular a pair of genuine all-timers, and the Star Wars universe fits over that immaculate form like a bionic-armed Skywalker's black leather glove. "It's truly the perfect pairing," game director Greg Foertsch said, somewhat predictably, during a group presentation. "Honestly, you couldn't believe that this hadn't been done before." Indeed! With so much sci-fi owing a debt to Star Wars, and so many XCOM-alike tactics games leaning into sci-fi, and so many of developer Bit Reactor's team having come from XCOM studio Firaxis, Zero Company feels like several loops closing at once. In a way I could just leave things there: if you like either of these things, you'll like this game. If you like them both I suspect you'll love it.

"It's just XCOM Star Wars" is a bit reductive, I'll admit. There are differences, many of them little ones, some a little bigger. The good news is they work well, even if perhaps they dilute the absolute purity of certain XCOM-isms. (The golden "two action points for everyone" rule is a classic example of something that's been tweaked here).

Starting with that exterior Star Wars layer, the standout feature is a properly linear narrative. This is relatively light-touch - a lot of missions will just feel like typical missions, with only a couple, in the six or seven hours I played, playing out as specific narrative beats - meaning the replayability factor so essential to these games will hopefully remain preserved. But it also gives space for all the usual Star Warsiness you might expect.

You are, surprise, a scoundrel of sorts with a rag-tag crew that gets reluctantly reeled into something bigger. Elements of this have been done to death now when it comes to Star Wars properties, but a curious new brain worm-infested enemy faction, some dubious late-Republic intelligence officers, and the delightful southern drawl of your protagonist default Hawkes' voice (Hawkes is heavily customisable - I went for a Maul-like Zabrak, you could also be a Twi'lek, a human, and so on) and a bit of genuine rakish personality to the writing certainly helps. There's also an early outline of a decent, if light, noir-y thriller here, between the gangland Hutts, the dockyard secrecy and those intelligence officers.

1 of 3

Caption

Attribution

In your base you'll also find the other big departure from most XCOM-inspired games: you can walk around in third person, and in fact some missions, namely the narrative ones, will start with a few minutes of third-person exploration too. HQ-wise, it feels a bit like a smaller version of Destiny's Tower - or maybe more directly, Marvel's Midnight Suns' mansion - with static vendors and crew-members chilling at their usual stations, ready either for a casual bit of chit-chat or to reveal a bit of key info. Sometimes side missions might come up from this, such as one involving your former Republic Clone Trooper crewmate and a rescue mission for an old war buddy.

Much of the HQ-based metagame is familiar: various stations are upgradable or unlockable over time. The droid bay was inactive for much of my time, for instance; you can upgrade the medbay to have more beds, the armoury to have more weapons for sale, or head to a terminal to recruit more operators, and so on. These then feed into a nice system of resources, typically gained from - naturally - going on missions, whereby you can spend more credits to upgrade how many operators you can have in total. It's a classic turn-based tactics loop, and a classic for a reason, because it's hugely moreish.

There are some twists within it, mind. One of the biggest evolutions to the formula is the addition of 'bonds' between your operators, including your main character, which has a nice thematic tie-in to the whole "rag-tag crew" thing Star Wars loves so much (and the sense of attachment and jeopardy genre fans equally love from their games - this gives you even more reason to break down in tears at the loss of a long-term operator). It works relatively simply: operators who go on missions together earn XP towards levelling up their bond; when that's levelled up they get a skill point and a chance to do some Cross Training (not the gym group thing) where you choose from a few different minor passive buffs, such as +4 HP to both, or +3 to ranged damage, and so on.

1 of 3

Caption

Attribution

That, in turn, plays into another new-ish system called Operations. These are a kind of pre-mission appetiser, where you spend a resource called Intel - earned each cycle (day) and with a hard cap you can increase over time - to go on a little miniature text-based adventure. Typically you'll be given one of two or three options with semi-veiled outcomes, each offering small but, I suspect, eventually crucial rewards when you get further into the game and min-maxing your decisions becomes more important. On some occasions as I got further into the game, I faced specific 'dilemmas', where each of the four-ish options would increase the bond I had with some operators, and decrease it with others. On standard difficulty and this early in the game, I could get away with just annoying the dude I hired and had absolutely zero intention of bringing on a mission. But again, I suspect as you start taking casualties, either later in the game or on higher difficulties, this will become dramatically more important.

As for those missions, they're really just as you'd expect from a team like Bit Reactor: a nice mix of verticality, range, and varying, destructible cover, as well as a good range of enemy types even in the largely droid-focused early game. Each operator gets three action points here, with movement and firing weapons costing different amounts depending on the operator and their mode of attack. I chose to build my main guy as a sniper, for instance, so firing costs me two of my three points. With others, it was one, and some used a system where - as far as I could gather - they expended all the points they had left to fire an automatic weapon repeatedly.

Image credit: Eurogamer / EA

Another new system that plays into the sense of bonds and teamwork is 'assists'. A given operator selects the assist option, then the operator (within range) they want to assist them, then when they attack an enemy, the selected second person takes a shot too for free. Things like bonds and various character bonuses - each operator has a skill tree - can buff the effectiveness here. But smartly, these also play into various other bonuses you might be stacking as well, like damage from blasters and so on. Quickly, you can start to see how building one operator specifically as an assist-based machine, coupled with another high damage-dealer, can enable you to dramatically punch above your weight as encounters get trickier.

Likewise, there's a nice mix of general abilities to use in combat. You can assign equipment, from passive-buff weapon mods to active-use grenades, to your operatives beforehand, but they also come with their own abilities. My marksman Hawkes, for instance, could use an action point to steady himself before firing, increasing crit chance and chance to hit. Or he could fire a guaranteed-hit shot from his sniper rifle. Or give another nearby character an extra action point that turn. A character called Jae, meanwhile, who joins you a few hours in (and can optionally be deployed in missions as with any other operator), has a nice ability where she fires a finisher shot at any enemy below a certain amount of HP after your allies have attacked.

1 of 6

Caption

Attribution

You also see these improvements start to manifest in enemies as you progress: Super Battle Droids will take a turn to charge up a fairly powerful rocket, for instance, giving you something to focus on (or evade) when it comes back to your turn, while other enemies will make heavy use of grenades and the like, naturally. There's also a system I encountered later on in my playthrough whereby the big bad enemy faction gradually levels up over time. Your intelligence-gathering might grant you the chance to sabotage one of their two buffs while it's still being researched or constructed, but you'll have to live with what's left over for the rest of the game - another thing that plays in nicely to that replayability and sense of role-play that's so important for these games.

Missions, too, have a nice variety to them, even in the early stages I played. Sometimes you'll need to rescue someone within a set number of turns, or assign an operator to crack a safe, or operate some big crane remotely to provide your team with an escape route. All of them ultimately fit the usual mould, but the variety of them - and variety of locations, thanks to Star Wars' natural range of planets - made the dozen or so I played feel different enough.

And that, in a sense, is all Star Wars: Zero Company needs to do. It just needs to be different enough, to stand out a bit from the usual turn-based tactics fare, and to do more than treat Star Wars as a mere aesthetic. And from these first few hours it does so almost flawlessly. If you're anything like me, it's exactly what you'd hope for after hearing the premise. It's XCOM Star Wars. It's based on the sensational foundations of that series and made by people who evidently, thoroughly, get it. And it really is a perfect match.

title: An Israeli Satirist’s Bid to Save His Country’s Democracy
author: @NewYorker
content:
Lior Schleien is often referred to as Israel’s Jon Stewart, a comparison that amuses him, since it exaggerates his small country’s standing even more than his own, but he’ll take it. Schleien, who is forty-eight, was born and grew up in Tel Aviv; he earned a master’s degree in law, but in the early two-thousands he turned his focus to comedy, writing a satirical column for the newspaper Maariv and appearing on a prime-time TV show. Soon, he was hosting a late-night talk show, “Halayla” (“Tonight”), for which he won the Israeli equivalent of an Emmy, in 2008. He then created and hosted two hit programs: “Matzav Ha’Uma” (“The State of the Nation”), which began in 2010, the year after Benjamin Netanyahu returned to the premiership, following a decade out of the office; and a successor show, “Gav Ha’Uma” (“The Nation’s Backbone”), which he also produced and ran from 2015 to 2020. His programs featured elements similar to those of Stewart’s “Daily Show”: a monologue, riffs on the news, a supporting panel of “pundits,” and a not quite playful interview segment with leading politicians and officials—including, in 2014, with Netanyahu himself, who then sought exposure among hipper voters.

Actually, Schleien had voted for Netanyahu more than once, when he was younger. (As a teen-ager, in 1994, he had been in central Tel Aviv when a Hamas suicide bombing on a nearby bus killed twenty-two people. “I belonged to the strong right, not to the weak left,” he said.) By 2014, however, he had “grown up” and was ensconced in Tel Aviv’s live-and-let-live culture with his partner, Merav Michaeli, a feminist activist and a Labor Party member in the Knesset. (She served as the Party leader from 2021 to 2024; the couple now have three young children.) And as Netanyahu’s coalitions hardened Schleien’s programs became edgier, skewering Netanyahu sycophants in the Likud Party, anti-élitist demagogues, cultic settlers, and rabbinic mandarins. Schleien, like Stewart, had become a sapper in a culture war he did not seek. “I saw myself doing satire—television, standup, books, films—until I died, not a player on the court but a referee,” he told me. For years, as a showrunner, he was the one in the writers’ room who “argued for playing it cool”: “Let’s make fun of them, get paid, take the applause, and come back tomorrow for another day’s work.” But, he added, “With this government, that ain’t the case anymore: we are being led to a hellhole.”

Schleien isn’t on broadcast television anymore, either. His shows were cancelled for what writers for Ynet and Haaretz considered questionable reasons, among them alleged pressure from Netanyahu’s allies, although the networks involved named other justifications, including financial ones. But Schleien has responded with a coruscating online presence, emerging as less of a jester and more of a conscience for Israeli liberals. In this crucial election year, he is arguably the most effective, and certainly the most daring, opposition voice in the country.

Schleien’s shows landed because, like all great satire, they presupposed a commonwealth of decency and reasonableness—and the liberty to mock violations of it. But, outside of cosmopolitan sections of Tel Aviv, Herzliya, and Haifa, the liberalism that fuelled his humor couldn’t be taken for granted. Politicized Judaism has enabled the most egregious violations of that freedom—in the form of the militant Religious Zionist Party and ultra-Orthodox parties, which are part of Netanyahu’s coalition, and their educational institutions, which are based in Jerusalem and increasingly provide ideological grounding to the Israeli right. (On a Times of Israel podcast, the Tel Aviv University economist Dan Ben-David recently cited a study that found that the state provides a roughly thirty-eight-billion-shekel subsidy for ultra-Orthodox communities, which, he said, is a third more than it spends on hospitals and public research universities combined.) For Schleien, these have been major foils.

In Jerusalem’s Old City, for example, the Western Wall, which abuts the site of the destroyed Judean temple, is still frequented by pilgrims, tourists, and visiting dignitaries, including American politicians, who typically slip handwritten messages in between its stones. But in recent years it’s become a shrine for religious zealots, who march there in the thousands on Jerusalem Day, often menacing Arab shopkeepers along the way. So, one year, to counter that politicized piety, Schleien had the cast of “Gav Ha’Uma” dress up as “Wizard of Oz” characters and dance to the Wall while singing a made-up Hebrew version of “We’re Off to See the Wizard.” Schleien was equally impatient with the paid official state rabbinate, which oversees rabbinic courts and has guarded its right—first established under the British Mandate—to certify marriages, divorces, burials, and dietary laws. This entails handing out thousands of patronage jobs to rabbis, bureaucrats, undertakers, and inspectors. In a 2019 monologue, Schleien featured clips of a sermon by a retired chief rabbi, Yisrael Meir Lau, in which he extolled the ingenuity of medieval Talmudic sages for their method of determining a woman’s virginity, which involved, grotesquely, having her sit on a barrel of wine.

Mocking the Wall and a former chief rabbi took some cheek, especially because Lau is a Holocaust survivor, and because religious devotion may have seemed a secondary target at the time, given the security threats that Israel was facing: Iranian hostility, rockets from Gaza and Lebanon. But Schleien considers official pietism—the theocratic strictures, the holy geographies, and Iron Age notions of vengeance—a threat in its own right, and one that exacerbates various security crises. In 2016, on “Gav Ha’Uma,” he grilled the settler leader Bezalel Smotrich, now Netanyahu’s finance minister, who had argued for building a new Jewish temple on the Mount adjacent to Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, and who has said that Jerusalem will reach Damascus. “You realize,” Schleien told him, referring to the boycott movement against Israel, “how you are prompting more antisemitism, and more B.D.S.?”

But Schleien has been correspondingly irritated by self-styled “centrist” politicians, such as Yair Lapid and Benny Gantz, who, though secularists themselves, coddled the religious establishment purportedly in the interests of national solidarity—what Gantz’s party has called “consensus and unity”—but in what was widely interpreted as blatantly pandering to their voters. For Schleien, centrists are so “desperate for the ‘middle center,’ or ‘extreme center,’ that one can find political room, not to the left and right but only up and down.” When, in 2020, “Gav Ha’Uma” was taken off the air, it was “a knife in the back of secularism,” Ram Fruman, the founder of the Secular Forum, said in Haaretz. “Management claimed it was for financial reasons,” Schleien told me, “much like, but before, Stephen Colbert—our clock runs ahead of America’s.”

So Schleien turned to standup comedy and to posting videos on YouTube that continued where his programs had left off. In 2022, when a new election was in the offing, he co-founded the online channel Relevant. Netanyahu was returned to power in the fall; in January, 2023, he began an assault on the judiciary, aiming to subordinate the Supreme Court to his Knesset majority. That move prompted months of mass demonstrations, and Schleien’s videos added to their impact. After the October 7th massacre, he tempered his tone. By the spring of 2024, however, Netanyahu’s assault on Gaza seemed to be endless, ruthless, governed by no diplomatic strategy—sacrificing civilians and hostages alike—and the Biden Administration was repeatedly cautioning the Israel Defense Forces about “humanitarian law.” Schleien returned to form.

He created a video for Relevant about President Isaac Herzog’s visit to the state-supported Bnei David academy, in the West Bank settlement of Eli, where, augmented by Torah studies, young Israelis train to join the I.D.F., many of them as officers. (Some forty per cent of graduates from infantry-officer schools have a national religious background.) In his talk, Herzog—another erstwhile “centrist”—condemned the “groundless hatred” and the “divisions” that had roiled the nation before October 7th, implying that it was the pro-judiciary demonstrators, not theocratic settlers, like those in the audience, who had somehow weakened the country. Schleien intercut video of a sermon by the head of Bnei David, Rabbi Eliezer Kashtiel, who had notoriously suggested that Arabs had “genetic problems,” and thus were better off under occupation. Kashtiel also criticized women’s equality, and he weighed in on Gaza: “Even if the residents of Gaza had come to us with flowers and love letters full of hearts,” he said, “it would have been our obligation,” even on the Sabbath, “to start the war to conquer the Land of Israel.”

In the video, Schleien added that the settlers and the whole religious apparat “force us to fund their way of life”—incomes, hence taxes, in Tel Aviv are generally far higher than those in Jerusalem and the settlements—“and force us to die in their religious wars.” (The ultra-Orthodox do not serve in the Army, and the Supreme Court’s ruling, in 2017, that they must is what initially precipitated the government assault on the judiciary.) “Unity is a lovely word, a good feeling,” Schleien said, “but we know from math class that, if one side of the equation is positive and the other is, in the same measure, negative, what they have between them is—nothing.”

Relevant closed in late 2024, but last November Schleien launched an online movement, called Free Israel, a play on the slogan “Free Palestine,” and released videos, he told me, aimed at influencing public opinion so that Israel can “free itself first from Netanyahu’s rule.” Soon after, he met with a group of secular and orthodox students in a military-preparatory program in the West Bank settlement of Susya, and, after his session, a counsellor who mentored a group of “hilltop youth”—young settlers who defiantly camp on West Bank heights hoping to establish yet more settlements—challenged Schleien to take on his more rightist audience, inviting him to a question-and-answer session with his own group. Schleien accepted.

The dialogue was respectful and unusually penetrating. The counsellor argued that “faith and roots”—adhering to religious law, based on rabbinic interpretations of the Talmud, and pursuing the settlement of the promised land—yielded “a staying power” that secular Jews lacked. Schleien countered, “I’m connected to my Judaism, to Israel, Zionism, and Hebrew culture no less than you, and maybe somewhat more,” since he is always weighing the extent of his “Jewishness and Israeliness,” and doesn’t “live according to a book.” Besides, he said, “My four grandfathers and grandmothers fled here to avoid being murdered.” In fact, the original Zionist pioneers were mainly secularists who “kicked against religion even before coming here,” Schleien said, to build “a new Judaism.”

The video became a sensation, viewed, in segments, more than two and a half million times. Since then, Schleien has continued his campaign, which he and a few friends have financed, to meet with dozens of groups of Israeli youth—some seven hundred thousand of whom will be voting for the first time in the fall and who, in their majority, identify as “right wing.” He also engaged in lengthy discussions with Assaf Sharon, a professor of philosophy at Tel Aviv University who studied for several years in a settlement, and Avner Inbar, who are the founders of the liberal think tank Molad, and with Alissaa Symon, a scholar affiliated with it, to explore Israel’s democratic crisis. There are now more than ninety Free Israel videos, with more than sixty million views, in whole or in part, across social-media platforms, and Schleien has a waiting list of more than six hundred groups requesting a meeting. “I won’t get to all of them, but it’s nice to be asked,” he told me.

I attended two tapings, at which Schleien, readied like a shortstop, fielded predictable questions: How can he still want two states? How can Arabs be part of a “Jewish state”? Can secularism not be carried to an extreme? (“As if there is such a thing as ‘secular extremism’—what, defending, too fiercely, critical rationality and the freedom to choose?” he told me.) But Schleien has empathy for his young audiences. They are, he says, sheltering from missiles and dealing with a government that incites them to hatred. “They’re told that, if we just keep bombing the whole Middle East, then God—who is Jewish and on their side—will fix everything. It’s hard on them.”

What appears to be hardest on Schleien, perhaps, is the effect that Israel’s recent crises are having on people in other countries, particularly the United States. When, immediately after the Hamas attack, he heard young Americans chanting, “From the river to the sea,” whether they properly understood the meaning of the slogan or not, he feared that many American progressives, who traditionally have felt empathy for Israeli progressives and supported the secular democracy that they have long espoused, have ironically bought into the image of Israel projected by its far right, and that to them the idea of “a Jewish and democratic state” has become a contradiction in terms.

In fact, one of Schleien’s Free Israel videos was directed at American liberals, after a group of Hollywood actors and other film workers signed a letter pledging to boycott some institutions within the Israeli film industry. Schleien’s video was a plea for help, but also for recognition. “You don’t have to sabotage Israeli art and culture and academia and businesses,” he said. “Netanyahu’s government has already got that covered.” The point, as Schleien sees it, is to defeat this government, not the people and the institutions that are striving for a democratic country. ♦

title: How War Has Redefined Marriage in Gaza
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Next to rubble and pictures of the deceased, people in Gaza are still getting married. Athar Abu Samra reports on why couples are refusing to delay their nuptials. With so much already lost, and so much still under threat, families in Gaza are seizing moments of joy wherever they can. Marriage ceremonies are no longer what they once were—nor do they express hope in quite the same way—but they have become powerful testaments to resilience.

As I worked on this story, I came to understand that the war has not only transformed weddings in Gaza. It has transformed people’s relationship with time itself. Before the war, marriage followed a familiar sequence. People finished their education, found work, built or rented a home, saved enough money and only then began planning a wedding. Families often postponed marriages until those expectations had been met. But now no one has that luxury — the luxury of time.

I spoke with one mother who had lost several of her children during the war, yet hurried to arrange the marriage of her youngest son. She told me she had always dreamed, like any mother, of watching all of her children grow up, get married, and fill her home with grandchildren. The war had taken much of that dream away, but she was determined not to lose what remained.

title: In Stunning Color, a Celestial “Treasure Chest” Full of Stars
content:
Attention space pirates: The latest jaw-dropping image from the James Webb Space Telescope—deservedly given Picture of the Month status from NASA, the Canadian Space Agency, and the European Space Agency—features a cosmic “treasure chest” right in its center.

Featured Video

That’s the nickname given to the picture by its publishers, and you can see why: The visual is dominated by a glowing, orange trunk, which is called a cometary globule. These gigantic clouds of gas and dust often take the shape of comets, with denser and darker heads leaving fainter trails behind them. However, they’ve got nothing to do with comets—they just have a similar appearance.

In this case, the head of the “comet” looks like the lid of an opened box. Scientists aren’t exactly sure how cometary globules are created in every scenario, but their origination typically requires the energy and radiation of young stars being formed inside of them. You can see it here as bright dots inside the treasure chest.

Around 70 stars are thought to be inside of the chest, with the largest being a rare O-type star about 19 times as massive as the sun. These stars are super-big, super-hot, and super-bright—and of great interest to researchers. Astronomers believe the star cluster is around 1.3 million years old, meaning the stars are still finding their way through the clouds of dust that surround them.

It’s all part of the Carina Nebula, which, in turn, is part of the constellation Carina, around 7,500 light-years away from Earth. It’s a particularly large and complex nebula, first discovered in 1752, and it’s one of five cosmic objects currently under observation by the James Webb Space Telescope.

Read more: “A Look Back at Hubble’s Most Breathtaking Images”

The treasure chest shape, though, is actually partly the result of something beyond the frame: the radiation and stellar winds being pumped out by the Eta Carinae star system, 39 light-years to the northwest, and another nearby system called Trumpler 16. They both contain incredibly big and bright stars—one in Eta Carinae is 100 times more massive and 5 million times more luminous than the sun—and they’re actively stripping away the lighter, less dense dust and gas from this region of space.

It’s likely that the chest began as a much bigger celestial area, driven by the star treasure inside, before being stripped down by external forces and chiseled into this particularly stunning shape.

title: Polyzonia is an ecosystem sim about breathing life into the Amazon rainforest until it can look after itself
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Featuring nature's best friend, the capybara

How about we get in our digital grass touching for the day? Well, I suppose we can't just yet, as Polyzonia, an ecosystem sim set in the Amazon rainforest, isn't out just yet, but it has caught my eye at the very least.

There's an immediate Spore-like quality to be found in Polyzonia, judging by its trailer at the very least. Not in the birthing of an alien lifeform kind of way, more the starting out with nothing and breathing life into something bit by bit. Everything comes down to clicks. After choosing one of a number of biomes, you add plant life to it here and there. When you've got enough of that to start with, you introduce animals, helping them live out their lives. You might click on a capybara so it can poop before you then click on a jaguar so it can eat the capybara.

It's even possible to focus on the micro, clicking on individual flowers to help pollinate them, contributing to their cycle of life. Or maybe you prompt some frog spawn hanging on a branch to fall into a river to turn into a tadpole, and subsequently a frog. This is all just the starting point though, as eventually the ecosystem starts to be able to run itself through automation, "until the rainforest can sustain and develop on its own."

The game's Steam page makes it sound like the devs are trying to be quite mindful of the flora and fauna in the game, noting that "plants and animals are not decorations, they interact with the world around them and you can influence them." There is this objectification that happens in video games whereby people create a sense of distance between themselves and what's on screen, forcing characters and animals alike into particular circumstances because there's no real-world material consequences. So I'm quite keen to see whether Polyzonia is successful in allowing its animal denizens to live a respectful, even if sometimes dangerous, life.

There's no release date attached to Polyzonia just yet, but you can wishlist it on Steam while you wait.

title: Indie game publisher Devolver Digital wants to go private, believes current share price "does not reflect the true market value" of the company
author: Connor Makar
content:
Exit the gungeon.

Indie game publisher Devolver Digital is looking to return to private ownership, after a rough few years as a publicly-traded company.

In a press release sent to investors, Devolver Digital said that it didn't believe the current share price did not "reflect the true market value" of the company.

Devolver Digitals believes it has "faced the ongoing challenge of delivering growth in line with market expectations despite those difficult sector conditions," pointing to wider industry turmoil since it went public back in 2021.

When the company went public, it was valued at £694.6m, or roughly $950m. Since then, the share price has dropped by 96.27 percent, bringing the value of the company down to around £34.64m / $46.63m.

Whether or not Devolver Digital will return to private ownership depends on its shareholders, who will vote on the decision on the 8th September during the company's annual general meeting. If they vote yes, Devolver Digital will go private on the 16th September.

In a statement to Gamesindustry.biz, a spokesperson for Devolver Digital said: "Devolver and its board are seeking shareholder approval to delist, believing becoming a private company is in the best interests of Devolver, its employees, its partners, and its Shareholders as a whole.

"We’ve made an announcement about this. The purpose is simple and positive. Being private will allow the Devolver Digital team, especially the finance, legal, and executive team, to singularly focus on the long-term health of the company and less on satisfying the requirements of the public market, which have nothing to do with being a successful game publisher."

If the company does go private, it is estimated the company will save around $1.6m per year. It is no secret that the stock market has been tough on video game companies following the COVID-19 pandemic, which kept people inside and resulted in a spike of industry growth. Since then, layoffs have been a common occurrence at even the largest companies.

Devolver Digital has continued to publish games during this period of stock-related rockiness, including the excellent Cult of the Lamb and Skate Story.

title: 'To own a Razer Artisan Keycap is to display one’s allegiance, a mark of belonging within the Cult of Razer' says the PR nonsense behind this $90 coil of snakes
author: Andy Edser
content:
"To own a Razer Artisan Keycap is to display one’s allegiance, a mark of belonging within the cult of Razer," says the marketing gumph for the company's first artisan keycap. I've read a lot of ambitious press releases in this job, but that's definitely the strangest sentence I've parsed this year.

That being said, I do like the look of the Razer Artisan Keycap - Triple-Headed Snake Edition. Because as the name suggests, it's made up of a twisting coil of snakes. Indiana Jones wouldn't approve, but as for Andy-ana Edser? Aye, it's alright by me.

Razer's slippery new keycap is resin-cast, has been individually hand-painted (I'd genuinely enjoy that job), and subjected to a two-stage quality control process that makes sure no dust or bubbles are left on the final product.

It's been designed to fit on MX-style, cross-stem switches, so it should be compatible with most keyboards. Even if you haven't bought into the cult of Razer and gone for a competitor's product instead. Which is probably some form of heresy in Razer's eyes, I would imagine.

The keycap is also "the next step towards the ultimate expression of keyboard customisation," and "a statement of identity," apparently. My goodness. There was me thinking it was a little trinket you could shove on one of your lesser-used switches and admire on occasion between games.

If you want one for yourself, Razer has a signup form for the initial batch on the product page, complete with a neon-green countdown timer that wouldn't look out of place in NASA mission control. In much smaller font underneath is the price: $90, which makes it one of the most expensive keycaps I think I've ever covered on this site.

"One of a kind. One of the cult," says Razer. Sure thing. Can I just enjoy my pricey keycap in peace, instead?

title: O EMPIRE! WARD OFF THY ROT puts you in an abandoned, dithered world with a cursed object and asks you to do one thing: survive the journey
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Hark!

Do you remember, or do you even know, about the Game Boy Camera? It's exactly as it sounds, a little camera attached to an original Game Boy cartridge that you could plug in and take photos with. You could even get a printer! The aesthetic therewithin is a particular one, utilising a tiny 128x128 pixel sensor, the end result being an incredibly dithered and pixelated yet charming look. There are few games that capture such a vibe, but O EMPIRE! WARD OFF THY ROT, a game about carrying a cursed object through an abandoned world, might just manage to.

Specifically, it comes across as if miniature, stop-motion sets are being filmed from a bird's-eye view (you can have a gander in the teaser trailer below, but a big seizure warning is in order). As cute as I might make that sound, the feeling is more one of dread, a tilt shift effecting lightly obfuscating sections of the world until you approach them. In O EMPIRE! WARD OFF THY ROT (a title that one must capitalise on every occasion), you are a lone traveller, who for some reason has to take a cursed object… somewhere, all the while attempting to survive whatever comes your way.

The world isn't barren, but it certainly isn't filled with life, and it sounds like the journey will be long: "The game is a slow, journey-driven survival experience focused on travel rather than combat. Stamina and supplies must be managed as you traverse long distances on foot through ruins, roads and bleak terrain," explains the game's Steam page. "Knowing when to push forward or retreat is central to progression."

A tension also appears to come from the very object you have to carry, as it can influence your movement and decision-making, "becoming increasingly difficult to carry." Your progress is also dictated by how much you have travelled, what resources you've acquired, and your endurance over time, all of which adds up to a fine balancing act. I'm curious as to how this plays out in practice, the trailer also shows something related to the ability to equip rings, I'm just not entirely sure what that means.

O EMPIRE! WARD OFF THY ROT doesn't have a release date, but you can wishlist it on Steam in the meantime.
